summary:
We built IGNIS 0G, an interactive web platform for exploring how flames ignite, spread, and go out in microgravity. We organized NASA research into a searchable catalog and digitized 336 published test runs from FLEX-1, BASS-II, and Saffire I–III, covering everything from burning fuel droplets to flame spread aboard a spacecraft.

The platform lets users compare individual runs side by side and find studies relevant to specific oxygen concentrations, pressures, airflow speeds, and gravity levels. An AI assistant answers questions using the research catalog and links to the original sources so users can verify the evidence.

Fire behaves differently in microgravity, and understanding those differences matters for spacecraft safety. IGNIS 0G helps researchers and engineers find relevant experimental evidence more quickly and gives students and educators a way to explore the science using real NASA data.
details:
We built IGNIS 0G, an interactive web platform for exploring how fire behaves in microgravity. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, the project brings published NASA combustion research into one place so users can find relevant experiments, compare individual test runs, and trace findings back to the original reports.

Why it matters. On Earth, hot gases rise and stretch a candle flame upward. In microgravity, this buoyancy-driven flow weakens, and a flame can become nearly spherical when airflow is low. Oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and the material being burned all affect how a fire behaves. Understanding these differences matters for spacecraft fire safety, from choosing cabin materials to studying how flames spread or go out.

What we built. We digitized 336 published NASA test runs across three programs: 276 FLEX-1 fuel droplet tests, 47 BASS-II tests on solid materials, and 13 Saffire I–III test records from experiments aboard Cygnus cargo spacecraft. Each record preserves the reported measurements, units, and a reference to its source table. The platform lets users compare up to four individual runs side by side and export selected data as CSV or JSON.

How it works. A user investigating how airflow affects flame spread can enter conditions for oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and gravity. IGNIS 0G ranks studies by how closely those inputs match the ranges reported in the literature. It checks each parameter separately, so a study can be relevant even when the exact combination of conditions has yet to be tested. Users can then open the individual runs and see what NASA measured under the actual test conditions.

The platform also includes an AI research assistant that uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It searches indexed NASA sources for relevant passages and gives those passages to a language model to draft an answer with citations. The system checks the citation references and can report when the available evidence is insufficient.

IGNIS 0G is designed for researchers and engineers looking for experimental evidence and for students and educators exploring combustion through real flight data. Our next step is to add more NASA datasets and test the research workflow with users.
